title: The Goddess of bees
hookLine: no creature with two legs or four could kill the demon, so the Goddess came as a swarm of bees; her promise to return
carry: the mother comes back, in any form
tomorrow: Krishna's conch came from the bottom of the sea. how?
last: SHIVA AND SHAKTI CAN'T BE SPLIT.

lines: NOTHING WITH TWO LEGS OR FOUR.
SO SHE CAME COVERED IN BEES.
cards: A demon named Aruna wanted to be unbeatable. So he prayed and fasted for years, until the creator god Brahma granted him a boon. In the way it's usually told: no creature with two legs or four could ever kill him.
Not gods, not people, not animals. Then he drove the gods out of heaven. They fought, and nothing with two legs or four could touch him.
So the Goddess came. Covered in bees.

teach.b: Bees in her hands, bees in her hair, bees pouring out of her in a dark, humming cloud. Six legs each. The swarm covered Aruna and his army, and that was the end of the unbeatable demon.
She's called Bhramari, the Goddess of bees, and she was promised in advance.
The Devi Mahatmya, the great poem of the Goddess sung at Navaratri, has her say that when Aruna troubles the worlds, she'll take the form of countless bees, and be praised as Bhramari.

teach.h: WHENEVER TROUBLE RISES, I WILL COME.
teach.b: A few lines later comes the bigger promise: whenever trouble rises, I will come down and end it. That's the teaching. For many Hindus, God is also Mother, Devi, and she doesn't stay far off.

teach.h: GOD AS MOTHER, WHO COMES BACK.
teach.b: She comes back, again and again, in whatever form the trouble needs, even the smallest. At Srisailam in South India, she's still worshipped as Bhramaramba, mother of the bees.

teach.h: BHRAMARA, A BEE: BREATHE IN, HUM OUT.
teach.b: Now the breath that shares her bees' name: bhramari, from bhramara, a bee. Many teachers today keep it simple: a quiet in-breath through the nose, and a long, low hum out, mmm, for as long as the out-breath lasts.
Lips closed, teeth slightly apart, jaw loose. To turn it inward, rest your thumbs lightly on the little flaps at the front of your ears and close them.

teach.h: THE MOTHER COMES BACK, IN ANY FORM.
teach.b: The room disappears, and the hum is all inside. Plenty of people hum when they're scared or can't sleep. A Hindu who knows this story hums knowing who once came as a hum.

how: Hindus praise the Goddess as Bhramari in hymns, and at Srisailam she is worshipped as Bhramaramba, mother of the bees. In yoga practice, bhramari, the humming bee breath, is done by breathing in through the nose and humming out, often with the ears closed by the thumbs, commonly before meditation.

o: a mind that buzzes from thought to thought
a whistling breath through rounded lips
the bee: the Goddess who came as a swarm, and the humming breath

games.q: match the story to the teaching.
p: the demon with the two-legs-or-four boon
the Goddess who came as bees

s: the Devi Mahatmya promises the Goddess will come as countless bees
and be praised as Bhramari. then: whenever trouble rises, I will come.
in Hindu teaching, God is only ever pictured as a father
many Hindus worship God as Mother, Devi, who comes back again and again.
you need to press hard on your ears for the hum to work
keep it light. the thumbs just close the ear flaps.

games.q: your little cousin asks why the Goddess came as bees this time, and not riding her lion. what fits today's teaching?
o: because the trouble needed it: the demon's boon left out six-legged things, and she comes in whatever form is needed.
because bees belong to a different, smaller goddess who isn't Durga at all.
because the gods ran out of weapons and the bees turned up by accident.
games.why: the Mother comes back in whatever form the trouble needs, even the smallest.

practice: Lips gently closed, jaw loose, breathe in through the nose and hum on the out-breath, low and steady, until it runs out; if you like, close the ear flaps with your thumbs and hear the hum inside.
Some people offer the hum to the Goddess; it works as plain sound, too, and if you can't make noise where you are, hum silently and feel the lips tingle anyway.
After a few rounds, let the humming stop and sit in the quiet it leaves.

wordCard.voice: Bhramari. From bhramara, the bee. The Goddess who came as a swarm, and the breath that hums like one.

orig.note: Sanskrit: of the bee, from bhramara, a large bee.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: the mother comes back, in any form. Even as a swarm of bees. That's day one hundred one.
